items.d: India **130 of 193**, value **0.685** — 'medium' band, at the doorstep of 'high'. Composite of life expectancy at birth, mean + expected years of schooling, and GNI per capita (PPP). Value has risen from 0.434 (1990) → 0.685, a 53% gain. Best line for 'growth is not development'.
India loses roughly **30% of its HDI value** when discounted for inequality in health, education and income — the loss itself is the argument, not the rank.

India **102 of 193**, value 0.403 — measures maternal mortality, adolescent birth rate, seats in parliament, secondary education and LFPR. India's weakest limb is female labour force participation, not education.

India **131 of 148**, ~64.1% of the gap closed. Strong on political empowerment (historically top-20 on that sub-index), near the bottom on economic participation and health & survival. Note the divergence between GII and GGGI — different constructs, use the right one.

Headcount fell **24.85% (2015-16) → 14.96% (2019-21)**; **24.82 crore** Indians exited multidimensional poverty between 2013-14 and 2022-23. 12 indicators across health, education, standard of living — Alkire-Foster method.
items.s: NITI Aayog National MPI & Discussion Paper, 2024

items.d: At $2.15/day (2017 PPP), India's poverty rate fell **27.1% (2011-12) → 5.3% (2022-23)**; about **171 million** people lifted out. The single strongest poverty-decline statistic available.

India still has the **largest absolute number of multidimensionally poor** — around 234 million — even as the rate falls sharply. The rate-versus-absolute-number contrast is a ready-made nuance point.
India **116 of 174**, score **0.49** — a child born today will be only 49% as productive as one with full health and education. Bank stopped updating it, so cite as 2020 vintage.

India **118 of 147** — measured on GDP per capita, social support, healthy life expectancy, freedom, generosity and perceived corruption. Useful in well-being/GDP-critique answers alongside Bhutan's GNH.

India **105 of 127**, score **27.3** — 'serious'. Built on undernourishment, child stunting, child wasting and child mortality. **India officially contests it**: three of four indicators are child-specific and the undernourishment estimate rests on a small opinion poll — say this and you have both the fact and the critique.

items.t: SOFI — State of Food Security and Nutrition
items.d: About **13.7% of Indians undernourished** (~195 million, the world's largest number); **over half the population cannot afford a healthy diet**. The affordability figure is the sharper one for food-security answers.
India's child wasting rate is among the **highest in the world (~18.7%)** — wasting is acute, recent under-nutrition, distinct from stunting (chronic). Getting the distinction right earns the mark.

**57% of women (15-49)** and **67% of children (6-59 months)** anaemic — both *worse* than NFHS-4. Rare case where a health indicator moved backwards; use it against 'India's nutrition story is uniformly improving'.

India **176 of 180**, one of the lowest scorers — 58 indicators over climate, ecosystem vitality and environmental health. India rejects the weighting, which penalises low per-capita emitters for absolute totals. Pair with per-capita emissions to make the equity argument.

India in the **top 10 (10th)** — among the best-performing large economies, on very low per-capita emissions and rapid renewable growth. Top three ranks are always left vacant. Use as the counterweight to EPI 176.

India **5th most polluted country** (improved from 3rd); **Byrnihat (Meghalaya) the most polluted city in the world** and **Delhi the most polluted capital**; **13 of the 20** most polluted cities globally are Indian. PM2.5 far above the WHO 5 µg/m³ guideline.

India is the **3rd largest emitter in absolute terms (~7-8% of global)** but per-capita emissions ~**2 tCO₂e against a world average of ~4.7** and a US figure ~14. Historical cumulative share under 4%. This trio is the CBDR-RC argument in one line.
India **63 of 120**, and among the few countries improving on all three dimensions — system performance, security, and transition readiness.

India is among the **most climate-vulnerable large economies**; over **80% of the population lives in districts vulnerable to climate hazards** and about 27 crore people are exposed to extreme heat risk.

India **39 of 133**, up from **81 in 2015** — the steepest sustained climb of any large economy; **1st among lower-middle-income countries** and 1st in Central & South Asia. Strong on ICT services exports and market sophistication, weak on institutions and R&D spend.

India **38 of 139**, up from 44 (2018) and 54 (2014); infrastructure score improved sharply. Anchor for PM Gati Shakti and the National Logistics Policy target of cutting logistics cost to single-digit % of GDP.

The **EoDB ranking was scrapped in 2021** after a data-manipulation audit (India's last rank: 63 of 190, up from 142 in 2014). Replaced by **B-READY (Business Ready)**. Citing EoDB as a live rank is a factual error — cite the discontinuation instead, it reads better.
India **39 of 67** — measured on economic performance, government efficiency, business efficiency and infrastructure. India's weakest pillar is infrastructure.

India is the **3rd largest startup ecosystem** in the world — **1.6 lakh+ DPIIT-recognised startups** across 800+ districts, **100+ unicorns**, and roughly **half of recognised startups have at least one woman director**. Nearly 45% come from tier-2/3 cities.
India **49 of 133**, and 1st globally on AI-related sub-indicators like AI talent concentration and ICT services exports.

India ranks **1st in the world in AI skill penetration** and is among the top three in AI talent concentration and GitHub AI project contributions — but lags badly on private AI investment and compute.
India in **Tier 1 ('role-modelling')**, score **98.49/100** — assessed on legal, technical, organisational, capacity-development and cooperation measures.

groups.g: Governance, democracy and rule of law

items.d: India **96 of 180**, score **38/100** (scale: 0 highly corrupt, 100 very clean) — a perception index of expert and business assessments, not measured corruption. That methodological caveat is itself a scoring point.

India **41 of 167**, score ~**7.18**, classified a **'flawed democracy'** — scored on electoral process, civil liberties, government functioning, political participation and political culture. India scores highest on electoral process and participation.

India **79 of 142** — eight factors including constraints on government powers, absence of corruption, open government, fundamental rights, order and security, and civil and criminal justice. India's weakest: civil justice (delay).

India **151 of 180**, improved from 159 — assessed on political, economic, legislative, social and safety indicators. India's economic indicator (ownership concentration, ad dependence) is the weakest limb.

India's composite score rose **57 (2018) → 66 (2020-21) → 71 (2023-24)**. Kerala and Uttarakhand top at 79; no state is now in the 'aspirant' category. Domestic, NITI-built, and far more citable in an Indian answer than the global SDR rank.
India around **109 of 166**, score ~64 — pulled down by SDG 2 (hunger), SDG 3 (health) and SDG 5 (gender). Contrast with the NITI index to show how construct choice drives the rank.
India **116 of 163** — militarisation, societal safety and ongoing conflict. Useful only as a scene-setter; the sub-indicator on internal conflict is the usable part.
India **14th of 163** and rated 'high impact'; deaths from terrorism in India have fallen substantially over the decade, with LWE-affected districts down from 126 to 38.
India has an estimated **11 million people in modern slavery** — the largest absolute number globally, though a mid-range prevalence rate. Anchors bonded labour and trafficking answers.

India is now the **4th most-represented country** with 54 universities ranked; IIT Delhi (123) and IIT Bombay (129) lead, IISc tops on citations per faculty. No Indian institution in the global top 100 — the gap is research output and international faculty/students.
India **39 of 119** — highest among lower-middle-income economies, strong on natural, cultural and non-leisure resources, weak on tourist service infrastructure and health & hygiene.

India has **44 World Heritage properties** — 36 cultural, 7 natural, 1 mixed (Khangchendzonga) — **6th highest in the world**. Latest additions: Santiniketan and Hoysala temples (2023), Moidams of Charaideo (2024), and the **Maratha Military Landscapes** (2025).

**15 elements** on UNESCO's Representative List — Kutiyattam, Vedic chanting, Ramlila, Ramman, Chhau, Kalbelia, Buddhist chanting of Ladakh, Sankirtana, Thatheras of Jandiala Guru, Yoga, Kumbh Mela, Durga Puja in Kolkata, Garba of Gujarat and others.
**91 Ramsar sites** covering ~1.36 million ha — the **largest network in Asia** and third largest in the world, up from 26 sites in 2014. Tamil Nadu leads with the most sites.

sections.h: India in Numbers — The Macro Spine

groups.g: Size, growth and structure of the economy

items.d: India is the **4th largest economy** at ~**$4.19 trillion** nominal, having crossed Japan in 2025; **3rd largest by PPP** at ~$17 trillion. Projected to be 3rd nominal by 2027-28. Share of world GDP ~3.6% nominal, ~7.9% PPP.
Real GDP growth **6.5% in FY25**, with FY26 projected at **6.5%** — fastest among major economies. Decadal average ~6.6%. India contributes about **16% of global growth**.

Per capita net national income ~**₹2.35 lakh (~$2,880)** in FY25, roughly doubled in nominal terms in a decade. GNI per capita keeps India in the **lower-middle-income** band (World Bank threshold for upper-middle is ~$4,500) — the 'Viksit Bharat 2047' target implies reaching ~$14,000, a 5x rise.

Services ~**55%**, Industry ~**28%**, Agriculture ~**16-18%** of GVA. The structural anomaly: agriculture holds **46.1% of employment** for ~18% of output, while services generate 55% of output on ~30% of employment. That mismatch *is* the disguised-unemployment argument.

Manufacturing stuck at ~**17% of GVA** against the **25% target** of the National Manufacturing Policy 2011 and Make in India — 'premature deindustrialisation'. India skipped the manufacturing-led transition that East Asia used.

About **90% of the workforce is informal** and the informal sector produces ~**45% of GVA**; **e-Shram** has over **30 crore** registrations of unorganised workers. Formalisation is measured by EPFO additions (~1.3 crore net in FY25) and GST registration.

MSMEs contribute ~**30% of GDP**, ~**45% of exports**, and employ ~**23 crore** people across **6+ crore** units on Udyam. The 'missing middle': over 99% are micro, and firms deliberately stay small to avoid regulatory thresholds.

groups.g: Public finance — Budget and fiscal position

items.d: **4.4% of GDP** budgeted for FY26, down from 9.2% in FY21 (COVID peak) and 4.8% in FY25 — the glide path now targets a **declining debt-to-GDP ratio** rather than a deficit number, a doctrinal shift from the FRBM Act's deficit anchor.

**₹11.21 lakh crore** capex in FY26 BE (~3.1% of GDP), up ~4x from FY20; plus **₹1.5 lakh crore** of 50-year interest-free capex loans to states. Capex multiplier is ~2.45 against ~0.98 for revenue expenditure (NIPFP/RBI) — the argument for quality of spending.

Total expenditure ~**₹50.65 lakh crore** in FY26 BE. Biggest claims on the rupee: **interest payments (~20%)**, states' share of taxes (~22%), central sector schemes, defence, and subsidies. Interest payments exceed the entire capex budget — the debt-servicing constraint in one line.

Centre's gross tax-GDP ~**11.7%**, general government ~**18%** — well below the OECD average (~34%) and below peer emerging economies (~24%). Direct:indirect tax split has moved to roughly **57:43**, a progressivity gain.

Budget 2025-26 made income up to **₹12 lakh effectively tax-free** in the new regime (₹12.75 lakh for salaried, with standard deduction) — foregone revenue ~₹1 lakh crore, aimed at reviving urban consumption.

Gross GST **₹22.08 lakh crore in FY25**, up 9.4%; monthly record **₹2.37 lakh crore (April 2025)**. Average monthly collection has roughly doubled since FY21. Registered taxpayers ~1.5 crore, from 65 lakh at launch.

The Council collapsed the four-slab structure into **5% and 18%**, with a **40% demerit rate** for sin and luxury goods — the most significant GST reform since 2017, aimed at ending classification disputes and inverted duty structures.

Centre's debt ~**57% of GDP**, general government ~**81%** — high by emerging-market standards but overwhelmingly **rupee-denominated and domestically held**, which is why India avoids the currency-mismatch crisis that hits other high-debt economies. External debt ~19% of GDP.

Major subsidies in FY26 BE: **food ~₹2.03 lakh crore**, **fertiliser ~₹1.67 lakh crore**, petroleum small after decontrol. Food + fertiliser together exceed the health and education budgets combined — the standard 'merit vs non-merit subsidy' framing.

The **15th Finance Commission** fixed states' share of the divisible pool at **41%** (down from 42% on J&K's reorganisation). Cesses and surcharges — outside the divisible pool — have risen to a substantial share of gross tax revenue, which is the states' core grievance. **16th Finance Commission (Arvind Panagariya)** reports for the 2026-31 cycle.

Record **$824.9 billion** in FY25 — merchandise **$437.4 bn** plus services **$387.5 bn**. Services now carry nearly half of India's export earnings, and India is the **7th largest services exporter** in the world.

Merchandise trade deficit ~**$283 billion**, but the services surplus and remittances hold the **current account deficit at ~0.6% of GDP** — well inside the 2.5% comfort threshold. Services + remittances are India's external shock absorber.

Crude oil (~$130-140 bn), gold, electronics and **edible oil (~$17 bn)** dominate imports. Crude import dependence is ~**88%**, natural gas ~50%, and edible oil ~**57% of consumption** — three structural vulnerabilities to name in any energy or food-security answer.

**USA is India's largest trading partner** (~$132 bn bilateral) and the largest export destination; **China is the largest source of imports**, with a bilateral deficit exceeding **$99 billion** — the single largest deficit India runs with any country.

**Gross FDI $81.04 billion in FY25** (+14%); cumulative inflows since April 2000 crossed **$1 trillion**. But **net FDI collapsed to under $1 billion** as repatriation and disinvestment surged — the gross/net divergence is the sophisticated point. Top sources: Singapore, Mauritius; top sector: services and computer software; top state: Maharashtra.
~**$690 billion**, peaking at $704.9 bn — the **4th largest reserves** in the world, covering roughly 11 months of imports. Gold's share in reserves has risen sharply as central banks diversify.

**$129.4 billion** in 2024 — the **world's largest recipient** for a decade running and about 14% of global remittances; India was the first country to cross $100 bn. The source mix has shifted from Gulf blue-collar to US/UK/Singapore white-collar.

The rupee trades around **₹85-88/$**; **Special Rupee Vostro Accounts** now permit rupee settlement with several countries, and India has signed local-currency-settlement arrangements with the UAE and Indonesia. Rupee's share in global forex turnover remains ~1.6%.

**1.46 billion** — the world's most populous country since 2023. Median age ~**28-29** (China 40, Japan 49); **~65% below 35**; working-age share peaks around **68% in the 2030s** — the demographic dividend window closes around 2055.

**2.0 and now ~1.9** — **below the replacement level of 2.1**. Bihar highest (~3.0), Sikkim/West Bengal lowest (~1.1-1.6). India's population will still grow to ~1.65 billion by 2060 because of **population momentum** — that term is the mark.

The 60-plus share rises from ~**10.5% (2022) to ~20.8% by 2050** — the elderly will outnumber children under 15. Kerala and Tamil Nadu have already aged; Bihar and UP have not. **Feminisation of ageing**: women outlive men, so the elderly are disproportionately widowed women with no pension.

**31.1% urban at Census 2011**, ~36-37% now, projected **40% by 2030 and ~50% by 2050** — adding roughly 400 million urban residents. Cities already generate over **60% of GDP** on 3% of land. India's urbanisation is under-counted: 'census towns' remain governed as villages.

Reference date **1 March 2027** (1 October 2026 for snow-bound areas); **houselisting phase April-September 2026**; conducted under the **Census Act, 1948**, with confidentiality of individual records. Two firsts: **caste enumeration, the first since 1931**, and a **digital census with self-enumeration**. It also unfreezes **delimitation**, frozen by the 84th Amendment until the first census after 2026.

Sex ratio at birth improved to ~**930-940 females per 1,000 males** (SRS/NFHS-5), and the overall sex ratio is now above 1,000 in NFHS-5 — but the *child* sex ratio remains the weak point, and Haryana and Punjab remain the worst-performing large states.

Roughly **45 crore internal migrants** (Census 2011, ~37% of the population); the 2017 Economic Survey's Cohort-based Migration Metric put annual inter-state migration at **~90 lakh**. Uttar Pradesh and Bihar are the largest sources; Delhi, Maharashtra and Gujarat the largest destinations. COVID-19 exposed the invisibility of this workforce — 'one nation one ration card' was the policy answer.

**LFPR 60.1%**, **WPR 58.2%**, **unemployment 3.2%** (usual status, 15+). The low headline unemployment number coexists with high underemployment — the meaningful indicator in India is not UR but the **quality of work**, since self-employment dominates.

items.t: FLFPR — Female Labour Force Participation Rate
items.d: **23.3% (2017-18) → 41.7% (2023-24)** — nearly a doubling, the single most striking labour statistic available. But the rise is driven largely by **rural self-employment and unpaid family work**, not by paid formal jobs — state the trend *and* the caveat.
**Self-employed 58.4%**, regular wage/salaried 21.7%, casual labour 19.8%. The share of regular salaried work has *fallen* since 2018-19 — the informalisation trend inside the formal narrative.

Rose from **42.5% (2018-19) to 46.1% (2023-24)** — a *reversal* of structural transformation, reflecting distress absorption after COVID rather than agricultural revival. A powerful counter-intuitive data point.

Youth (15-29) unemployment ~**10.2%**, and much higher among the educated — graduate unemployment is multiples of the illiterate rate. This is the **educated-unemployment paradox**: unemployment rises with education level, pointing to skill mismatch, not job scarcity alone.

Only about **4-5% of the workforce has formal vocational training** against 52% in the US, 68% in the UK and 96% in South Korea. India needs to create roughly **78.5 lakh non-farm jobs annually** to 2030 to absorb the workforce.

**77 lakh gig workers (2020-21) → projected 2.35 crore by 2029-30**, then 4.1% of the total workforce. The **Code on Social Security, 2020** was the first Indian law to define 'gig' and 'platform' workers; Rajasthan and Karnataka legislated first at state level.
items.s: NITI Aayog, 'India's Booming Gig and Platform Economy', 2022

items.d: Government health expenditure **1.84% of GDP** against the **National Health Policy 2017 target of 2.5% by 2025**. India is among the lowest public health spenders globally — the root cause of the out-of-pocket burden.

Fell from **62.6% (2014-15) → 39.4% (2021-22)** of total health expenditure — a genuine structural improvement, driven by PM-JAY, Jan Aushadhi and public spending. Still far above the ~18% global average. Health costs push ~5-6 crore Indians into poverty annually.

**97 per lakh live births (2018-20)**, down from 130 (2014-16) and 556 (1990) — India met the MDG and is on track for the **SDG target of 70 by 2030**. Kerala ~19; Assam, UP and MP remain far above the national figure.

**IMR 28** and **U5MR 32** per 1,000 live births — both have more than halved since 1990. Neonatal deaths now form the bulk of infant mortality, shifting the policy problem from immunisation to institutional delivery quality.

Doctor-population ratio ~**1:811**, better than the WHO norm of 1:1000, but **nurses at ~1.7 per 1,000** against the WHO norm of 3 and hospital beds ~**1.3 per 1,000** against 3. The shortage is of nurses, beds and rural placement — not doctors in aggregate.

Only **23.4% of Class 3 children can read a Class 2 text** (up from 16.3% in 2022) and **33.7% can do subtraction** — improvement post-COVID but still a learning crisis. NIPUN Bharat targets universal foundational literacy and numeracy by 2026-27.

**24.8 crore** school students; GER near 100% at elementary, **77.4% secondary**, **56.2% higher secondary**; dropout is concentrated at the secondary stage. PTR ~25:1 against the RTE norm of 30:1 — the aggregate is fine, the distribution is not.

Enrolment **4.33 crore**, **GER 28.4%** against the **NEP 2020 target of 50% by 2035**; female GER has overtaken male; **SC/ST/OBC enrolment rising fastest**. India has 1,100+ universities and 45,000+ colleges, but ~60% of colleges are rural and single-stream.

~**4.6% of GDP** against the **6% recommended by the Kothari Commission (1966)** and reaffirmed by **NEP 2020** — a target unmet for six decades. That is the cleanest 'policy continuity without delivery' example in the education syllabus.

**~97 crore internet subscribers** and ~116 crore telecom connections; **teledensity ~84%**, but rural teledensity ~59% against urban 130% — the digital divide is now about *quality and use*, not access. India has among the world's lowest data tariffs.

**18-19 billion transactions a month**, worth **₹24-25 lakh crore**; UPI accounts for nearly **half of all real-time digital payment transactions in the world**. Live in seven-plus countries including UAE, Singapore, France, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Mauritius. The flagship Digital Public Infrastructure export.

**Aadhaar ~142 crore**; **Jan Dhan 55 crore accounts** (56% women, ~₹2.6 lakh crore deposits); DBT has transferred through **1,200+ schemes** with cumulative estimated savings of **₹3.48 lakh crore** from removal of duplicate and ghost beneficiaries.

The digital economy is ~**11.74% of GVA (2022-23)**, projected to reach nearly **20% by 2030** — growing about twice as fast as the rest of the economy. Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) is now an explicit Indian export doctrine, carried into the G20 New Delhi Declaration.

**India Semiconductor Mission, ₹76,000 crore** — units approved at Dholera (Tata–PSMC fab), Sanand (Micron ATMP, CG Power, Kaynes), Morigaon Assam (Tata OSAT) and Jewar. **India's first indigenously packaged chip rolled out in 2025**. India currently designs ~20% of the world's chips but fabricates almost none.

**₹10,372 crore** over five years across seven pillars — compute capacity (38,000+ GPUs empanelled), foundation models, datasets (AIKosh), application development, future skills, startup financing and safe & trusted AI. India hosts the **AI Impact Summit in 2026**.

India's space economy ~**$8.4 billion (~2% of the global market)**, targeted at **$44 billion by 2033**. **100% FDI liberalised (2024)**, IN-SPACe as the single-window regulator, a **₹1,000 crore venture fund**, and 300+ space startups. Milestones: **Chandrayaan-3 (first at the lunar south pole, 2023)**, Aditya-L1, **SpaDeX docking (2025, 4th country to do it)**, **NISAR (2025, with NASA)**, Shubhanshu Shukla on Axiom-4 to the ISS (2025). Targets: **Bharatiya Antariksh Station by 2035, Indian on the Moon by 2040**.

sections.h: The Report Bank — Who Publishes What

items.d: Ministry of Finance, tabled a day before the Budget, authored by the **Chief Economic Adviser (V. Anantha Nageswaran)**. Recent themes: deregulation and 'getting out of the way', **AI and labour**, MSME compliance costs, and the observation that India must grow at **~8% sustained** for two decades for Viksit Bharat 2047. Always cite the theme, not just the growth number.

items.t: RBI Annual Report / Financial Stability Report
items.d: The FSR carries **GNPA of scheduled commercial banks at a multi-decade low (~2.5%)**, capital adequacy ~16-17%, and the stress-test results. The Report on Trend and Progress of Banking is the other pillar. Cite for anything on financial-sector health.

Article 151 requires the CAG's reports to be laid before Parliament and examined by the **Public Accounts Committee**. Landmark performance audits: 2G spectrum (2010), coal block allocation (2012), Ayushman Bharat (2023 — duplicate and invalid beneficiary IDs), and the audit that flagged the same mobile number registered against lakhs of beneficiaries.

SDG India Index, National MPI, Aspirational Districts/Blocks dashboards, Health Index, Export Preparedness Index, School Education Quality Index, Composite Water Management Index and the **Fiscal Health Index of States (2025)**. NITI is a **think tank without financial powers** — the contrast with the Planning Commission's allocative power is a standing PubAd point.

Annual, under MHA. Crime rate ~**422 per lakh**; crimes against women ~**4.45 lakh cases (66.4 per lakh)**, most under 'cruelty by husband or relatives'; **cybercrime 65,893 cases (+24.4%)**. Prison Statistics India: **occupancy 131%** and **undertrials 75.8%** of the prison population. NCRB counts only *registered* crime — under-reporting is the standing caveat.
items.s: NCRB, Crime in India 2022 / Prison Statistics India

items.d: IIPS, Mumbai for MoHFW. **NFHS-5 (2019-21)** is the current round: TFR 2.0, sex ratio, anaemia 57%/67%, stunting 35.5%, institutional births 88.6%, women's household decision-making 88.7%. **NFHS-6 fieldwork is under way.** Cite NFHS for anything on health, nutrition or gender at household level.

NSO, annual since 2017-18, quarterly for urban; **revamped from January 2025 to give monthly estimates for rural and urban**. Replaced the five-yearly NSS Employment-Unemployment Survey. Any employment figure you quote must carry the PLFS round.

Revived after an 11-year gap. **MPCE: rural ₹4,122, urban ₹6,996 (2023-24)**; the rural-urban gap narrowed from 84% to ~70%; the food share of consumption fell below 50% in rural India for the first time — a classic **Engel's Law** illustration. Also resets the CPI basket and poverty estimation.

items.t: ISFR — India State of Forest Report
items.d: Forest Survey of India, biennial. **Forest and tree cover 25.17%** of geographic area (forest 21.76%, tree 3.41%) against the **National Forest Policy 1988 target of 33%**. Mangroves ~4,992 km². Criticism: plantations and orchards count as 'forest cover', so the number overstates natural forest.

items.t: ASER — Annual Status of Education Report
items.d: Pratham, citizen-led, rural, since 2005 — the survey that made 'learning outcomes' a policy category. Reading and arithmetic levels, and in 'Beyond Basics' years, the digital and financial competence of 14-18 year olds.

**India Justice Report** (Tata Trusts) ranks states on police, judiciary, prisons and legal aid — Karnataka has led recent editions. **NJDG (National Judicial Data Grid)** gives live pendency: **~5.29 crore cases**, of which ~4.6 crore in district courts.

groups.g: Global reports and who issues them

items.d: **AR6 Synthesis Report (2023)**: warming already ~1.1-1.2°C; the 1.5°C carbon budget will be exhausted in the 2030s at current rates; **'deep, rapid and sustained' cuts** required. WG-I physical science, WG-II impacts/adaptation, WG-III mitigation. **AR7 cycle is under way.**

Current NDCs put the world on track for ~**2.6-3.1°C** by 2100; closing the gap needs a ~42% cut in annual emissions by 2030. The 'Adaptation Gap Report' is its twin — adaptation finance needs of developing countries are **10-18 times** current flows.

items.t: WMO State of the Global Climate
items.d: **2024 was the warmest year on record and the first calendar year above 1.5°C** of pre-industrial warming; the last decade is the warmest ten-year period recorded; ocean heat content and sea-level rise at record highs.

items.t: IMF WEO and World Bank GEP
items.d: The **World Economic Outlook** (April/October) and **Global Economic Prospects** (January/June) carry the growth projections you cite for India versus the world. Both currently place India as the **fastest-growing major economy**.
Global FDI trends and India's position among the top 15 FDI recipients; also the source for greenfield project announcements, where India has ranked among the top three destinations.

items.t: IEA World Energy Outlook / India Energy Outlook
items.d: India will account for the **largest share of global energy demand growth to 2030**; the India Energy Outlook is the standard citation for the claim that India's energy demand will grow faster than any other country's.

WEF, published before Davos. Recent editions rank **misinformation and disinformation as the top short-term global risk**, and extreme weather and ecosystem collapse as the top long-term risks — a ready-made intro for AI, media or climate essays.

Only about **17% of SDG targets are on track** at the halfway point to 2030; the SDG financing gap for developing countries is ~**$4 trillion a year**. The two figures together frame any 'Agenda 2030' answer.

WWF, biennial — a **73% average decline in monitored wildlife populations since 1970**, steepest in freshwater species. Pair with the IPBES Global Assessment's **1 million species at risk of extinction**.

items.t: Human Development Report and thematic UN reports
items.d: **HDR** (UNDP, HDI/GII), **State of World Population** (UNFPA, population and rights), **State of the World's Children** (UNICEF), **World Employment and Social Outlook** (ILO), **Global Report on Trafficking in Persons** (UNODC), **World Drug Report** (UNODC), **Global Education Monitoring Report** (UNESCO). Matching the report to the right agency is itself a mark.

**Kudumbashree, Kerala** — 46 lakh women in a three-tier neighbourhood-group architecture linked to panchayats, running canteens, farming collectives and enterprise. *Lesson: women's collective action + livelihood diversification + embedding in local government is what converts a savings group into a governance institution.*

**DAY-NRLM / Lakhpati Didi** — 10 crore+ women in 90 lakh SHGs; the target of **3 crore Lakhpati Didis** (annual household income above ₹1 lakh) and 2 lakh+ **Bank Sakhis** and **Drone Didis**. *Lesson: the SHG platform, once built, can carry credit, extension, insurance and last-mile delivery — institutional infrastructure, not a scheme.*

**Amul / GCMMF, Gujarat** — 36 lakh farmer-members, turnover over ₹60,000 crore, and the model that made India the **world's largest milk producer (239 MT, ~24% of world output)**. *Lesson: aggregation + assured procurement + producer-owned processing beats fragmentation; the White Revolution's design is the template for FPOs.*

**Sahyadri Farms, Nashik** — 18,000+ farmer shareholders exporting grapes and processed fruit at scale. Central scheme target: **10,000 FPOs**. *Lesson: the answer to the 1.08-hectare average holding is aggregation of the market side, not consolidation of the land side.*

**Channapatna toys, Karnataka** and **Kutch embroidery (Shrujan)** — GI tagging plus design intervention plus e-commerce onboarding. *Lesson: GI protects the name; markets protect the artisan — protection without market access preserves poverty.*

**Hiware Bazar and Ralegan Siddhi, Maharashtra** — watershed treatment, a ban on water-intensive crops, and a crop plan fixed by the gram sabha turned drought-prone villages into ones with dozens of millionaire farmers. *Lesson: demand-side regulation by the community, not supply augmentation, is what makes a watershed programme stick.*
items.s: Popat Rao Pawar / Anna Hazare model

items.d: **Johads of Alwar (Tarun Bharat Sangh, Rajendra Singh)** — thousands of check dams revived five rivers including the Arvari. *Lesson: traditional water-harvesting plus community ownership can restore a river basin at a fraction of engineering cost.*

**Atal Bhujal Yojana** — the first scheme to make **community-prepared water security plans** the condition for incentive funds in seven water-stressed states. India's groundwater extraction stage is ~60% and agriculture uses ~**78-80%** of water. *Lesson: groundwater is a common-pool resource; only user-level institutions (Ostrom) can regulate it, not permits.*

**Sukhomajri, Haryana** — the first Indian experiment in **payment for ecosystem services**, where villagers received water rights in exchange for protecting the catchment. *Lesson: align private incentive with the commons and enforcement becomes self-executing.*

**Project Tiger** — tiger numbers **1,411 (2006) → 3,682 (2022)**, ~75% of the world's wild tigers, with voluntary relocation packages and eco-development committees. Contrast: **Niyamgiri**, where the gram sabhas rejected bauxite mining under FRA. *Lesson: conservation succeeds when the local community is a stakeholder, and fails when it is treated as an encroacher.*
items.s: NTCA / Orissa Mining Corporation v. MoEF (2013)

items.d: **Namami Gange** — sewage treatment capacity added along the main stem, Arth Ganga's livelihood model, and the return of dolphins to stretches of the river. Counter-example: **Bellandur lake, Bengaluru**, catching fire from untreated effluent. *Lesson: river cleaning is a sewage-infrastructure and enforcement problem, not a ritual or awareness problem.*

**Madhya Pradesh Lok Sewa Guarantee Adhiniyam, 2010** — the first Indian law to make timely service delivery an entitlement with a **penalty on the defaulting officer**; now replicated by 20+ states. *Lesson: citizen charters bind only when a default carries a personal financial consequence.*

**Andhra Pradesh's Society for Social Audit (SSAAT)** — an independent audit unit staffed by village social auditors, reading MGNREGA muster rolls aloud in the gram sabha. **Meghalaya Community Participation and Public Services Social Audit Act, 2017** made it statutory across departments. *Lesson: audit works when the auditor is independent of the implementing agency and the finding is read publicly.*

**CPGRAMS** — 20+ lakh grievances a year, average disposal time cut to about **13 days** from 28, with a feedback-based appeal. *Lesson: a grievance system is only as good as its independent appeal and its measurement of citizen satisfaction, not its closure rate.*

**Aspirational Districts Programme** — 112 districts ranked on 49 indicators across health, nutrition, education, agriculture, finance and infrastructure, with real-time dashboards and a 'competition + collaboration + convergence' design; extended as the **Aspirational Blocks Programme (500 blocks)**. UNDP called it a global model of local development. *Lesson: measurement + ranking + a dedicated officer moves outcomes without new money.*

**SVAMITVA** — drone survey of inhabited village land giving **property cards to over 2.4 crore** rural households, converting dead capital into collateral. Complement: **Bhoomi (Karnataka)** for tenancy records. *Lesson: de Soto's 'dead capital' argument, implemented — clear title is the precondition for rural credit.*

**One Nation One Ration Card** — portability of PDS entitlements for ~80 crore beneficiaries across all states, built after the migrant crisis of 2020. *Lesson: entitlements must follow the person, not the domicile, in an economy with 45 crore internal migrants.*

**Kerala's Janamaithri Suraksha** community policing and **Tamil Nadu's all-women police stations** (first in the country, 1992). Against these, **Prakash Singh (2006)** directives — Security Commission, fixed tenure, separation of investigation and law-and-order — remain only partially complied with by most states. *Lesson: reform blocked at the structural level can still advance at the operational level.*
items.s: Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006)

items.d: **Odisha, Cyclone Phailin (2013)** — 10 lakh evacuated, deaths in double digits, against **~10,000 in the 1999 super-cyclone**. The UN cited it as a global benchmark. Built on early warning + colour-coded evacuation + cyclone shelters + community volunteers. *Lesson: the shift from relief-centric to preparedness-centric management (DM Act, 2005) is measurable in lives.*

**Ahmedabad Heat Action Plan (2013)** — South Asia's first, with a colour-coded warning system, hospital preparedness and changed outdoor work hours; credited with preventing over a thousand deaths a year and now replicated in 20+ cities. *Lesson: a hazard becomes a disaster only through exposure and vulnerability — HAPs act on vulnerability.*

**CoWIN** — over 220 crore doses recorded on an open digital platform, offered as a global public good. *Lesson: DPI turns a logistics problem into a data problem — but only where connectivity and digital literacy exist, which is why the assisted-mode design mattered.*

**Mitticool** (clay refrigerator, Mansukhbhai Prajapati), **Jaipur Foot**, and **ISRO's Mangalyaan at ~₹450 crore** — cheaper than the film *Gravity*. *Lesson: 'jugaad' becomes innovation when it is standardised, certified and scaled — the constraint drives the design.*

**MKSS, Rajasthan** — the jan sunwai (public hearing) movement that read out muster rolls and bills in the village square and produced the **RTI Act, 2005**. *Lesson: a law can originate from a local practice; the practice was 'the right to know', the statute merely codified it.*

**Smart Cities Mission** — ₹1.64 lakh crore across 100 cities, completed in 2025, but implementation ran through **SPVs that bypassed elected municipal councils**, hollowing out the 74th Amendment. *Lesson: a delivery vehicle chosen for speed can weaken the constitutional institution it was meant to serve — always the strongest 'critically examine' point.*

items.t: Ambedkar, on the working of a constitution
items.d: "However good a Constitution may be, if those who are implementing it are not good, it will prove to be bad." — the standard opening for any answer on institutional decay versus constitutional design.

items.t: Ambedkar, on political versus social democracy
items.d: India enters a life of contradictions — **"equality in politics and inequality in social and economic life"** — one person one vote, but not one person one value. The single most usable quotation across GS-1 society, GS-2 rights and Essay.

Constitutional morality is **"not a natural sentiment; it has to be cultivated"** — invoked by the Supreme Court in *Naz Foundation*, *Sabarimala* and *Navtej Johar* to mean fidelity to constitutional values over majoritarian sentiment.
items.s: Constituent Assembly / Grote, cited in Sabarimala (2018)

items.t: Nehru, on the moment of independence
items.d: "At the stroke of the midnight hour, when the world sleeps, India will awake to life and freedom... a moment comes, which comes but rarely in history." — the *Tryst with Destiny* speech; also the source of "the service of India means the service of the millions who suffer."

The Constitution is **"first and foremost a social document"**, and its core provisions are aimed at furthering the goals of the **social revolution**. His other coinage — the **'seamless web'** of democracy, social revolution and national unity — is the standard frame for any 'basic features' answer.
items.s: The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation

items.t: Nani Palkhivala, on the Constitution's authorship
items.d: "The Constitution is not a mere lawyers' document; it is a vehicle of life, and its spirit is always the spirit of the age." — often paired with the judiciary's living-tree approach to interpretation.
"Law without justice is a body without a soul." Also his line that bail, not jail, is the rule — the anchor for undertrial and personal-liberty answers.

"Privacy is the constitutional core of human dignity... the right to be let alone." *Puttaswamy* also holds that **privacy is intrinsic to Article 21 and Part III as a whole**, not a stand-alone right.
items.s: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)

items.d: **"Development as freedom"** — development is the expansion of the real freedoms people enjoy, and poverty is **capability deprivation**, not merely low income. The intellectual basis of the HDI and of any 'growth is not development' argument.

"No famine has ever taken place in the history of the world in a functioning democracy" — famines are failures of **entitlement and exchange**, not of food availability. Use for food security, PDS and democratic accountability.

The **talisman**: "Recall the face of the poorest and weakest man whom you may have seen, and ask yourself if the step you contemplate is going to be of any use to him." — the antyodaya test, usable in ethics, governance and welfare answers alike.
"The earth provides enough to satisfy every man's need, but not every man's greed." — the standard sustainability epigraph, and the intellectual ancestor of the LiFE mission's sufficiency argument.

"The future of India lies in its villages" and his vision of **oceanic circles** — not a pyramid with the apex sustained by the base, but ever-widening circles with the individual at the centre. The philosophical case for the 73rd Amendment.

"Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high... into that heaven of freedom, my Father, let my country awake." Also his critique of nationalism as "organised selfishness" — useful for balance in nationalism essays.
"Dream is not that which you see while sleeping, it is something that does not let you sleep." — and "small aim is a crime", for essays on youth, education and aspiration.
items.s: A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, Wings of Fire

items.d: Sustainable development is development that **"meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs"** — the definition every environment answer should carry verbatim.
"Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely" — the classical case for checks and balances, separation of powers and independent oversight.

items.t: Madison, on government and human nature
items.d: "If men were angels, no government would be necessary. If angels were to govern men, neither external nor internal controls on government would be necessary." — the sharpest one-line justification for institutional accountability.
"It is getting to be harder to run a constitution than to frame one" — from *The Study of Administration* (1887), the essay that founded the discipline and the politics-administration dichotomy.

Bureaucracy is technically superior to any other form of organisation as **"the exercise of control on the basis of knowledge"** — but risks becoming an **'iron cage'** of rationality and 'a mechanism of dehumanised efficiency'. Both halves must appear in a balanced answer.

items.t: Sardar Patel, on the steel frame
items.d: The services are the **"steel frame"** of India, and the civil servant must have **"independence of expression and fearlessness"** and the freedom to speak the truth to the minister — the constitutional basis of Article 311 protection and of frank advice.

"In the happiness of his subjects lies the king's happiness; in their welfare his welfare... he shall consider as good, not what pleases him, but what pleases his subjects." — the oldest citable Indian statement of public interest over self-interest.

"It is the sceptre of the king that ensures the rain and the harvest" — and the Kural's rule that a just sceptre, not force, sustains the realm. A high-value Indian anchor when a Western thinker would be the obvious choice.

items.t: Justice Bhagwati, on public interest litigation
items.d: PIL is "a strategic arm of the legal aid movement... intended to bring justice within the reach of the poor masses" — the founding rationale of relaxed locus standi in *S.P. Gupta* (1981).
items.s: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981)

items.d: Caste is **"an enclosed class"**, sustained by endogamy; annihilating caste requires attacking the **religious sanction of the shastras**, and inter-caste marriage is "the real remedy". Also: "I measure the progress of a community by the degree of progress which women have achieved."
items.s: Annihilation of Caste, 1936 / Castes in India, 1916

items.d: The Satyashodhak Samaj (1873) and India's first school for girls (1848). Phule's *Gulamgiri* recast caste as slavery; Savitribai is the anchor example for women's education as the entry point to social reform.
***Stri Purush Tulana* (1882)** — the first modern Indian feminist critique, arguing that the faults blamed on women are equally men's. The earliest Indian citation available for a gender answer.

"Education is the most powerful weapon which you can use to change the world." Also: "A nation should not be judged by how it treats its highest citizens, but its lowest ones" — the prison-reform and marginalised-sections quotation.

items.t: Martin Luther King Jr., on justice
items.d: "Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere" and "the arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends towards justice" — for civil rights, dissent and social justice essays.
"Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains" — the social contract's opening, and the classical framing for liberty-versus-authority questions.

"Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached"; and his standard for religion — "they alone live who live for others". His Chicago address (1893) is the standard example of India's civilisational soft power.

Commons need be neither privatised nor nationalised — communities can self-govern them through **eight design principles**: clear boundaries, congruence with local conditions, collective-choice arrangements, monitoring, graduated sanctions, conflict-resolution, recognition of the right to organise, and nested enterprises. The single most citable framework for water, forest and fishery answers.

sections.h: Art, Architecture and Culture — Name It Precisely

items.d: Curvilinear **shikhara** crowned by **amalaka + kalasha**, raised plinth (**jagati**), no boundary wall, square garbhagriha with projections (**ratha**). Sub-styles: **Odisha** (deul + jagamohana — Lingaraja, Konark, Jagannath), **Khajuraho/Chandella** (clustered shikharas on a single platform, panchayatana), **Solanki** (Modhera Sun Temple with its stepped **surya kund**).

Stepped pyramidal **vimana**, octagonal **shikhara** at the apex, walled enclosure with a **gopuram** entrance, **mandapa** and temple tank. Evolution: Pallava (Mahabalipuram rathas, Shore Temple, Kailasanatha at Kanchi) → **Chola (Brihadesvara, Thanjavur, Rajaraja I, c. 1010, 60 m vimana)** → Vijayanagara-Nayaka, where the **gopuram outgrows the vimana** and kalyana mandapas appear.

Deccan hybrid — **Dravida elevation with Nagara curvature**; Chalukyas of Badami and Rashtrakutas, perfected by the **Hoysalas at Belur, Halebid and Somnathpur**: soapstone, **stellate (star-shaped) plan**, lathe-turned pillars, jagati platform and dense relief carving.

**Chaitya** = apsidal, barrel-vaulted worship hall with a stupa and a horseshoe **sun-window** (Karle, Bhaja, Ajanta 9 & 26); **Vihara** = residential cells around a courtyard. **Ellora** — 34 caves, uniquely **Buddhist, Hindu and Jain together**, with the **Kailasanatha (Cave 16), Rashtrakuta, 8th c., monolithic, carved top-down from living rock**. **Ajanta** — 29 caves, Buddhist only, murals in **tempera on a mud-plaster ground** (not fresco). **Elephanta** — Shaiva, the **Trimurti/Sadashiva**.

**Medhi** (drum) · **anda** (dome) · **harmika** · **yashti with chhatravali** · **vedika** railing with **four toranas** and the **pradakshina path**. Sanchi (Ashokan core, Sunga enlargement, Satavahana gateways), Bharhut, Amaravati (Satavahana, limestone medallions), Sarnath (Dhamek). **Aniconic phase**: the Buddha shown as footprint, empty throne, wheel or Bodhi tree — the image appears with **Gandhara (Greco-Roman, grey schist), Mathura (indigenous, red sandstone) and Amaravati (white marble)**.

**Delhi Sultanate**: arcuate style, **true arch and dome**, Qutb Minar and Quwwat-ul-Islam (Slave), Alai Darwaza (Khalji, first true dome and horseshoe arch), Tughlaqabad (austere, battered walls), Lodi tombs (double dome). **Provincial**: Gujarat (Sidi Saiyyed jali), Bengal (terracotta, curved 'do-chala' roof), Bijapur (**Gol Gumbaz, second largest dome, whispering gallery**), Mandu (Jahaz Mahal). **Mughal**: Humayun's tomb (first garden tomb, **charbagh**), Fatehpur Sikri (Buland Darwaza), **Taj Mahal (pietra dura, complete symmetry, riverfront charbagh)**, Shah Jahan's shift from red sandstone to **white marble**.

**Giridurga** (hill) — Rajgad, Raigad, Torna, **Shivneri**, Pratapgad, Salher; **Jaladurga** (island/sea) — Vijaydurg, Sindhudurg; **Vandurga** (forest) and **Sthaldurga** (plain). Features: **staggered right-angle gateways** to stop elephant charges, **machi** terraces, rock-cut cisterns, and a command shared between **havaldar, sabnis and karkhanis** so no one caste or family held a fort. **UNESCO inscribed the 'Maratha Military Landscapes' (12 forts) in 2025**.

**Eight recognised by Sangeet Natak Akademi**: Bharatanatyam (TN, from sadir/devadasi tradition, revived by Rukmini Devi Arundale), Kathak (UP, the only one with both Hindu and Mughal courtly lineage, gharanas — Lucknow, Jaipur, Banaras), Kathakali (Kerala, male, elaborate make-up), **Mohiniyattam** (Kerala, lasya), Odissi (tribhanga posture, Maharis), Kuchipudi (AP, dance-drama, Siddhendra Yogi), Manipuri (Ras Leela, Sankirtana), **Sattriya** (Assam, Vaishnavite monasteries of Sankardeva, recognised 2000). Chhau (Seraikella, Mayurbhanj, Purulia) is on UNESCO's ICH list.

**Bharata, c. 200 BCE-200 CE** — the treatise on drama, dance and music; source of **rasa (eight, with shanta added later by Abhinavagupta)**, **bhava**, **abhinaya** (angika, vachika, aharya, sattvika), and the **tandava-lasya** distinction. **Abhinavagupta's** *Abhinavabharati* is the great commentary; **Nandikeshvara's** *Abhinaya Darpana* the dance manual.

**Hindustani** — gharana-based, khayal, dhrupad, thumri, tarana; ten thaats (Bhatkhande). **Carnatic** — composition-centric, the **Trinity: Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar and Syama Sastri**; 72 melakarta ragas (Venkatamakhin). Common ground: raga, tala and the guru-shishya parampara. **Amir Khusrau** is credited with the sitar, tabla and the qawwali form.

**Murals**: Ajanta, Bagh, Sittanavasal (Jain, Pallava), Lepakshi (Vijayanagara). **Miniatures**: Pala (earliest, on palm leaf), Jain/Western Indian, **Mughal** (Persian technique + Indian realism; peaks under Jahangir with portraiture and natural history), **Rajasthani** (Mewar, Kishangarh's *Bani Thani*, Bundi), **Pahari** (Basohli's bold colour, **Kangra's** lyrical Krishna themes), **Deccani** (Bijapur, Golconda). **Folk**: Madhubani, Warli, Pattachitra, Kalamkari, Gond, Phad, Kalighat.

**Bhakti**: Alvars and Nayanars (Tamil, 6th-9th c.) → **Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita)**, **Madhva (Dvaita)**, **Basava (Lingayat/Virashaiva, vachanas)**, **Kabir and Nanak (nirguna)**, **Chaitanya (Bengal), Mirabai, Tulsidas, Surdas, Namdev, Tukaram, Narsinh Mehta**. **Sufi silsilas**: Chishti (Moinuddin Chishti at Ajmer, Nizamuddin Auliya — accepted no state patronage), Suhrawardi (accepted it), Qadiri, Naqshbandi. Both used the **vernacular**, rejected ritual hierarchy, and became vehicles of social critique.

**Six orthodox (astika)**: Samkhya (Kapila, dualism of purusha-prakriti), Yoga (Patanjali), Nyaya (Gautama, logic), Vaisheshika (Kanada, atomism), **Mimamsa** (Jaimini, ritual exegesis), **Vedanta** (Badarayana; Shankara's **Advaita**, Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita, Madhva's Dvaita). **Heterodox (nastika)**: Buddhism, Jainism, **Charvaka/Lokayata (materialist)**, Ajivika (Makkhali Gosala, determinism).

India has **600+ registered Geographical Indications** — Darjeeling tea was the first (2004). Handicraft GIs: Channapatna toys, Kanchipuram silk, Pochampally ikat, Banarasi brocade, Madhubani, Mysore silk, Kashmir pashmina. **UNESCO ICH: 15 elements**, including Yoga, Kumbh Mela, Durga Puja in Kolkata and **Garba of Gujarat (2023)**.

sections.h: History — Dates, Names and Turning Points

items.d: **c. 2600-1900 BCE** mature phase; over 1,500 sites, the largest Indian ones being **Rakhigarhi (Haryana), Dholavira (Gujarat — UNESCO 2021, water-harvesting reservoirs and a signboard), Lothal (dockyard), Kalibangan (ploughed field, fire altars), Banawali, Surkotada (horse remains debated)**. Features: grid town planning, **standardised burnt bricks in a 1:2:4 ratio**, the Great Bath, drainage, no monumental temples or royal tombs, and an undeciphered script.

**Chandragupta (321 BCE) with Kautilya**, Bindusara, **Ashoka (268-232 BCE)** — the **Kalinga war (261 BCE)** and the turn to **Dhamma**; edicts in **Brahmi, Kharosthi, Greek and Aramaic**, deciphered by **James Prinsep (1837)**. Administration: Arthashashtra's **saptanga theory**, mahamatras, dhamma mahamatras, rajukas, and the **Sarnath lion capital** as the state emblem. Megasthenes' *Indica*; Junagadh rock inscription of Rudradaman on the **Sudarshana lake**.

**c. 320-550 CE** — Chandragupta I, **Samudragupta (Prayag Prashasti by Harisena)**, Chandragupta II Vikramaditya (Fa-Hien's visit; the **Mehrauli iron pillar**). Achievements: **Aryabhata (zero, decimal place value, heliocentric hints, Aryabhatiya, 499 CE)**, Varahamihira, Kalidasa, the **Nalanda mahavihara**, Dashavatara temple at Deogarh and the Bhitargaon brick temple — the **first structural temples**. Also the beginnings of **land grants (agrahara/brahmadeya)** and, on one reading, of Indian feudalism.

**Cholas** — Rajaraja I and **Rajendra I (Gangaikonda Cholapuram, naval expedition to Srivijaya, 1025)**; the **Uttaramerur inscription** records **kudavolai** election to village sabhas, India's oldest documented electoral procedure; **nadu, ur, sabha, nagaram** as local bodies. **Vijayanagara (1336, Harihara and Bukka; Krishnadevaraya; Hampi)** and the **Battle of Talikota (1565)**; **amara-nayaka system**. **Pallavas, Pandyas, Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas, Satavahanas**.

**Sultanate 1206-1526** — Slave, Khalji (**Alauddin's market control and the first standing army**), Tughlaq (**Muhammad bin Tughlaq's token currency and capital transfer**; **Firoz Shah's** canals and jizya), Sayyid, Lodi; **iqta system**. **Mughals 1526-1857** — **Babur (Panipat I, 1526)**, Humayun, **Akbar (mansabdari, zabti/dahsala revenue with Todar Mal, Din-i-Ilahi, sulh-i-kul, abolition of jizya 1564)**, Jahangir, Shah Jahan, **Aurangzeb (reimposed jizya 1679, Deccan campaigns)**. **Shivaji's coronation 1674; ashtapradhan; chauth and sardeshmukhi**.

**Plassey 1757** (Clive, Mir Jafar) → **Buxar 1764** → **Diwani of Bengal 1765**, which gave the Company revenue authority and produced the **dual government**; **Regulating Act 1773**, **Pitt's India Act 1784**, **Charter Acts 1813 (trade monopoly ended except tea/China, ₹1 lakh for education), 1833 (Governor-General of India, end of commercial functions) and 1853 (open competition for the covered services)**; **Government of India Act 1858** transferred power to the Crown.

**Permanent Settlement (1793, Cornwallis, Bengal-Bihar-Odisha)** — zamindar as owner, fixed revenue, the **sunset clause**; **Ryotwari (Munro/Read, Madras and Bombay)** — direct settlement with the cultivator, periodically revised; **Mahalwari (Holt Mackenzie, 1822, North-West Provinces and Punjab)** — village or *mahal* as the unit. Consequence: **commercialisation of agriculture, sub-infeudation, and the rise of moneylender-driven indebtedness** behind the **Deccan Riots (1875)**.

**Dadabhai Naoroji's** *Poverty and Un-British Rule in India* (1901) and the drain theory; **R.C. Dutt's** *Economic History of India*; **M.G. Ranade** on industrialisation. Components: home charges, remittances, expenditure on Indian troops abroad and the trade surplus that bought nothing in return. **Deindustrialisation** of textiles and the shift to raw-material export — the economic critique that preceded the political demand.

**Revolt of 1857** — Mangal Pandey (Barrackpore, 29 March), Meerut (10 May), Bahadur Shah Zafar proclaimed; leaders Nana Saheb (Kanpur), Rani Lakshmibai (Jhansi), Begum Hazrat Mahal (Lucknow), Kunwar Singh (Bihar), Bakht Khan (Delhi). Causes ran from the **Doctrine of Lapse** and annexation of Awadh (1856) to the greased cartridge. Consequences: Crown rule, **Queen's Proclamation 1858**, army reorganisation on the **'martial races'** theory and one-third European ratio, and the end of annexation.

**Raja Rammohan Roy — Brahmo Samaj (1828)**, sati abolition (1829, with William Bentinck); **Derozio and Young Bengal**; **Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar** — Widow Remarriage Act 1856; **Dayanand Saraswati — Arya Samaj (1875)**, 'back to the Vedas', shuddhi; **Jyotirao Phule — Satyashodhak Samaj (1873)** and *Gulamgiri*; **Savitribai Phule** — first school for girls (1848); **Periyar E.V. Ramasamy — Self-Respect Movement (1925)**; **Narayana Guru — SNDP (1903)**, 'one caste, one religion, one God'; **Sir Syed Ahmed Khan — Aligarh movement (1875)**; **Annie Besant and the Theosophical Society**; **Vivekananda — Ramakrishna Mission (1897)**.

**Macaulay's Minute (1835)** and the downward filtration theory; **Wood's Despatch (1854)** — the 'Magna Carta of English education', vernacular primary schooling and the 1857 universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras; **Hunter Commission (1882)**; **Indian Universities Act 1904 (Curzon's control)**; **Sadler Commission (1917)**. Press: **Vernacular Press Act 1878 (Lytton)**, repealed 1882; **Newspaper Act 1908**, **Indian Press Act 1910**.

**INC founded 1885 (A.O. Hume, W.C. Bonnerjee presiding at Bombay)**. Moderates (1885-1905): Naoroji, Gokhale, Ranade, Pherozeshah Mehta — 'prayer, petition, protest', the constitutional method. Extremists (1905-1919): **Lal-Bal-Pal and Aurobindo** — swadeshi, boycott, national education, passive resistance. **Surat Split 1907**, reunion at **Lucknow 1916** with the **Lucknow Pact** between Congress and the Muslim League.

**1905** Partition of Bengal, Swadeshi; **1906** Muslim League (Dhaka), Calcutta session's swaraj demand; **1909** Morley-Minto — **separate electorates**; **1911** annulment of partition, capital to Delhi; **1915** Gandhi returns; **1916** Home Rule Leagues (Tilak and Besant); **1917** Champaran; **1918** Kheda and Ahmedabad; **1919** Rowlatt, **Jallianwala Bagh (13 April)**, Montagu-Chelmsford (**dyarchy**); **1920-22** Non-Cooperation with Khilafat, ended after **Chauri Chaura (Feb 1922)**.

**1927** Simon Commission (all-white) and the boycott; **1928** **Nehru Report** (dominion status, no separate electorates) and Jinnah's **Fourteen Points**; **1929** Lahore session — **Purna Swaraj**, 26 January 1930 as Independence Day; **1930** **Dandi March (12 March-6 April, 385 km)** and Civil Disobedience, **Dharasana satyagraha**; **1931** Gandhi-Irwin Pact and the Second Round Table; **1932** **Communal Award** and the **Poona Pact** (reserved seats in joint electorates instead of separate electorates for the Depressed Classes); **1935** Government of India Act — provincial autonomy, federation (never implemented), and the Reserve Bank.

**1939** Congress ministries resign; **1940** August Offer, Lahore Resolution (Pakistan); **1942** **Cripps Mission** ('a post-dated cheque'), **Quit India (8 August, 'Do or Die')**, and the **INA under Subhas Chandra Bose** (Azad Hind, 21 October 1943; the **INA trials at the Red Fort, 1945-46**, defended by Bhulabhai Desai, Tej Bahadur Sapru, Asaf Ali and Nehru); **1946** Cabinet Mission, Direct Action Day, **Naval Ratings' Mutiny**, Constituent Assembly convened 9 December; **1947** Mountbatten Plan (3 June), **Indian Independence Act (18 July)**, **Radcliffe Line**.

items.t: The peasant, tribal and worker movements
items.d: **Tribal**: Santhal Hool (1855-56, Sidhu-Kanhu), **Munda Ulgulan (1899-1900, Birsa Munda)**, Rampa rebellion (Alluri Sitarama Raju, 1922-24), Bhil and Koya uprisings. **Peasant**: Indigo revolt (1859-60), Deccan Riots (1875), Champaran (1917), **Kisan Sabha in Awadh (Baba Ramchandra)**, Moplah (1921), Bardoli satyagraha (1928, Vallabhbhai Patel earns 'Sardar'), **Tebhaga (1946-47)** and **Telangana (1946-51)**. **Workers**: AITUC (1920, Lala Lajpat Rai as first president).

**Integration of 565 princely states** by Patel and V.P. Menon through the Instrument of Accession — with **Junagadh (plebiscite), Hyderabad (Operation Polo, 1948) and Kashmir (Instrument of Accession, 26 October 1947)** as the exceptions. **Linguistic reorganisation**: Potti Sriramulu's fast and the creation of **Andhra (1953)**, the **Fazl Ali States Reorganisation Commission (1955)** and the **States Reorganisation Act, 1956** (14 states, 6 UTs), then Bombay's split (1960), Punjab-Haryana (1966), the North-Eastern reorganisation (1971-87), and **Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand (2000)** and **Telangana (2014)**.

**American (1776)** — 'no taxation without representation', Boston Tea Party (1773), the first written republican constitution with a bill of rights and federalism. **French (1789)** — Estates-General, Tennis Court Oath, Bastille (14 July), **Declaration of the Rights of Man**, liberty-equality-fraternity (the Preamble's source), the Terror, and Napoleon's **Civil Code (1804)**. **Russian (1917)** — February and October, Lenin's 'Peace, Land and Bread', the first socialist state, and the model for planned development India partly borrowed.

Britain first (c. 1760-1840) — coal, steam (Watt), textiles (spinning jenny, water frame, power loom), railways; consequences: **urbanisation, the factory system, child labour and the Mines Act 1842**, imperialism for raw materials and markets, and the intellectual reactions of **Adam Smith, Malthus, Ricardo and Marx**. For India: **deindustrialisation and the conversion into a raw-material supplier**.

**Germany** — Zollverein (1834), **Frankfurt Parliament (1848)**, Bismarck's blood and iron, unification 1871. **Italy** — Mazzini (Young Italy), Cavour (diplomacy), Garibaldi (Red Shirts), 1861/1870. **Ausgleich (1867)** creating Austria-Hungary. Compare with anti-colonial nationalism in Asia and Africa, which was **built against an external ruler rather than for internal unification** — the standard comparative point.

**WWI (1914-18)** — MAIN causes, Versailles (1919) and its war-guilt clause, the **League of Nations** and its failure of collective security. **WWII (1939-45)** — appeasement, Munich (1938), the **Atlantic Charter (1941)** and its self-determination promise, the **UN (1945)**, Bretton Woods (IMF and World Bank, 1944) and the **GATT (1947)**. **Decolonisation**: **UN Declaration on Granting Independence to Colonial Countries (1960)**, and the Suez crisis (1956) as the marker of the end of European primacy.

**Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan (1947-48)**, NATO (1949) and the Warsaw Pact (1955), Cuban Missile Crisis (1962), détente, and the collapse of the USSR (1991). **NAM** — **Bandung Conference (1955)** and the Panchsheel principles (1954, in the India-China Tibet agreement), founded at **Belgrade (1961)** by Nehru, Tito, Nasser, Sukarno and Nkrumah. India's post-1991 formulation is **strategic autonomy** and multi-alignment rather than non-alignment.

sections.h: Indian Society — Concepts, Thinkers and Data

items.d: **M.N. Srinivas** — a lower caste adopts the ritual, custom and ideology of a higher (usually 'twice-born') caste to claim upward mobility; **positional change without structural change**. Also his **'dominant caste'** (numerical strength, economic and political power, and ritual status) and 'vote bank'.

**Srinivas** distinguished **Westernisation** (changes from British contact — technology, institutions, values) from **Sanskritisation**; **Yogendra Singh's** *Modernization of Indian Tradition* argued India modernises **through tradition, not against it** — the best line for 'tradition versus modernity' questions.

**Louis Dumont** — *Homo Hierarchicus*: caste rests on the opposition of **purity and pollution**, and is an ideology of hierarchy rather than of stratification by power (criticised for ignoring power and for the Brahminical viewpoint). **G.S. Ghurye** — six features of caste: segmental division, hierarchy, restrictions on feeding and social intercourse, civil and religious disabilities, lack of unrestricted choice of occupation, and endogamy.

Caste is **'an enclosed class'** sustained by **endogamy**; it is not a division of labour but a **division of labourers** in a graded hierarchy — and its distinguishing feature is that it produces **'graded inequality'**, which prevents the lower orders from uniting. Annihilation requires attacking the **religious sanction**, and inter-caste marriage is 'the real remedy'.

**Verrier Elwin** initially favoured 'national parks' for tribes, later revised; **G.S. Ghurye** called them **'backward Hindus'** — assimilation; **Nehru's Panchsheel for tribes (in Elwin's *Philosophy for NEFA*)**: development along their own lines, respect for tribal rights in land and forest, training their own people, avoiding over-administration, and judging by the quality of human character evolved, not statistics. The current constitutional position is **integration, not assimilation or isolation**.

**Ranajit Guha (1982)** — Indian historiography was written from the elite's viewpoint (colonialist and nationalist alike); the subaltern has **autonomous consciousness and politics**. *Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India* (1983). Spivak's 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' is the critical turn.

**Rajeev Bhargava's 'principled distance'** — the state keeps a non-sectarian, context-sensitive distance from all religions, intervening where a religion violates rights (temple entry, triple talaq) and abstaining otherwise. Contrast: the American **wall of separation** and French **laïcité**. India's is **'equal respect for all religions' (sarva dharma sambhava)** rather than an absence of religion from public life.

**Bipan Chandra** — communalism is a **modern ideology**, not a survival of the medieval past, with three stages: (i) people of one religion have common secular interests; (ii) those interests differ from another religion's; (iii) they are **mutually hostile and irreconcilable**. Distinct from communal violence, which is its symptom.

**Paul Brass** on ethnicity as **instrumental**, mobilised by elites; **Selig Harrison's** 'dangerous decades' prediction on language, disproved by linguistic reorganisation. Types of regionalism: **supra-state (Dravidian), inter-state (river water, boundary), intra-state (Vidarbha, Bodoland)** and **secessionist**. India's response has been **accommodation through asymmetric federalism**, not suppression.

**Irawati Karve** — the four kinship zones (northern, central, southern, eastern), with the south permitting **cross-cousin and uncle-niece marriage** which the north prohibits under **sapinda and gotra exogamy**. The nuclear-family transition: **household size fell from 4.8 to about 4.4**, but the 'functional joint family' survives through remittances and care — 'nuclear in residence, joint in function'.

**SC 16.6% and ST 8.6% (Census 2011)**; OBCs estimated at **~41-52%** (NSS 61st round ~41%, Mandal's 52%) — no post-1931 caste census exists, which is why **Census 2027's caste enumeration** matters. Bihar's 2023 caste survey found **EBC 36% + OBC 27.1% = 63%**, and Telangana's 2024 survey put BCs at ~56%.

Crimes against SCs and STs run to **50,000+ and 10,000+ cases a year**, with conviction rates around 30-40% under the **SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989** (strengthened by the 2018 amendment reversing *Subhash Kashinath Mahajan*). **Manual scavenging** — prohibited by the 2013 Act, yet **hundreds of sewer and septic-tank deaths** continue; the **NAMASTE** scheme replaced Self-Employment Scheme for Rehabilitation.

**FLFPR 23.3% (2017-18) → 41.7% (2023-24)**; sex ratio at birth ~930; **only ~14% of Lok Sabha members are women**; women hold **~46% of panchayat seats**; women own under 15% of agricultural land while forming ~63% of the agricultural workforce; and Indian women perform **~7 times more unpaid domestic work** than men (Time Use Survey 2019). The **106th Amendment** reserves one-third of legislative seats after the census and delimitation.
items.s: PLFS / NSS Time Use Survey / NFHS

items.d: **31.1% urban (2011) → ~36-37% now → ~40% by 2030 and 50% by 2050**; 4,000+ statutory towns and **3,892 census towns** that remain governed as villages — India's 'hidden urbanisation'. Slum population ~6.5 crore (2011); cities generate over 60% of GDP; only ~20-25% of urban sewage is treated. **Migration**: 45 crore internal migrants (2011), with ~90 lakh inter-state annually.

**60-plus: 10.5% (2022) → 20.8% (2050)** — the elderly will outnumber children under 15; **feminisation of ageing** (women outlive men, so elderly women are disproportionately widowed and dependent); **elder abuse** reported by a significant share in HelpAge surveys; only about a quarter of the elderly have any pension. Instruments: **MWPSC Act, 2007**, the **Atal Vayo Abhyuday Yojana** and **Ayushman Bharat's 70+ universal cover**.

**Hindus 79.8%, Muslims 14.2%, Christians 2.3%, Sikhs 1.7%, Buddhists 0.7%, Jains 0.4% (Census 2011)**. Languages: **22 in the Eighth Schedule**, 121 languages and **270 mother tongues with more than 10,000 speakers**; six **classical languages** originally (Tamil, Sanskrit, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Odia), with **Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali added in 2024**. **43.6% speak Hindi** as mother tongue.

**MPI 24.85% (2015-16) → 14.96% (2019-21)**, 24.82 crore out of poverty; extreme poverty at $2.15/day **27.1% → 5.3%**. But the **top 1% hold 22.6% of income and 40.1% of wealth** (World Inequality Lab, 'the Billionaire Raj'), and consumption Gini is ~0.27 rural and 0.31 urban (HCES 2022-23). Present both — the decline in poverty and the concentration at the top are simultaneously true.
items.s: NITI / World Bank / World Inequality Lab

sections.h: Geography — Term Plus the Named Example

items.d: The **Indian plate moves north-east at ~5 cm a year**, colliding with the Eurasian plate — hence the rising Himalaya and the seismicity of **Zone V (North-East, Kashmir, Kutch, Andamans)**. **59% of India's landmass is earthquake-prone**. The **Deccan Traps** are flood basalt from the Reunion hotspot at the K-Pg boundary; the **Bhuj earthquake (2001)** occurred on an intraplate fault.

Three parallel ranges — **Greater Himalaya (Himadri)**, **Lesser Himalaya (Himachal — Pir Panjal, Dhauladhar, Mahabharat)** and **Shivalik**, separated by the **MCT** and **MBT**; longitudinal valleys called **duns** (Dehradun, Kotli dun) and the Kashmir **karewas** (lacustrine deposits, saffron). **Syntaxial bends** at Nanga Parbat and Namcha Barwa. Rivers older than the mountains cut **antecedent gorges** — Indus, Satluj, Brahmaputra.

Explanations: the **thermal (Halley) theory**, the **dynamic theory** — the **ITCZ** shift with the **Tibetan Plateau's heating**, the **Sub-Tropical Jet Stream's** withdrawal and the **Tropical Easterly Jet**, the **Somali/Findlater Jet**, and the **Mascarene High**. Modulators: **El Niño (deficit) / La Niña (surplus)**, the **Indian Ocean Dipole (a positive IOD offsets El Niño)**, **Madden-Julian Oscillation**, and **Eurasian snow cover (Blanford's hypothesis)**. Withdrawal from Rajasthan by September; the **retreating monsoon brings the North-East monsoon rains to Tamil Nadu (Oct-Dec)** — the reason Tamil Nadu's rainfall regime is anomalous.

**Kalbaisakhi/Nor'westers** (Bengal, pre-monsoon), **Bardoli Chheerha** (Assam), **Mango showers** (Kerala/Karnataka, aiding mango ripening), **Blossom showers** (coffee), **Loo** (northern plains), **Cherry blossom showers**, **Norwesters**, **October heat**, and **Western Disturbances** — extratropical cyclones from the Mediterranean that bring winter rain to the north-west, critical for the **rabi wheat crop**.

**Alluvial (~40% of the area, khadar vs bhangar)**, **Black/regur** (Deccan lava, moisture-retentive, self-ploughing, ideal for cotton), **Red and yellow** (crystalline igneous, iron-rich), **Laterite** (heavy rain and leaching, poor in humus, used as brick — Kerala, Karnataka), **Arid**, **Forest/mountain**, **Peaty/marshy** and **Saline/alkaline (reh, kallar)**. Degradation: **~30% of India's land is degraded** (ISRO's Desertification Atlas) — the number to quote for UNCCD questions.

**Upwelling** (nutrient-rich water rising, sustaining fisheries — the Somali coast during the SW monsoon), **thermocline**, **coral bleaching** (zooxanthellae expulsion above threshold temperature — the Gulf of Mannar and Lakshadweep), **atoll/fringing/barrier reefs**, **estuary versus delta** (Narmada and Tapi form estuaries because they flow through rift valleys with fast gradients), **tombolo, spit and lagoon** (Chilika — Asia's largest brackish lagoon; Vembanad — India's longest lake).

Form over water above **26.5°C** with low vertical wind shear and a **Coriolis force away from the equator (5°+)**; the **Bay of Bengal gets ~4 times more cyclones than the Arabian Sea** because of higher SST, freshwater-driven stratification and monsoon-trough interaction — though warming has increased Arabian Sea intensity. Anatomy: **eye, eyewall and rain bands**; **storm surge causes most deaths**, and IMD names storms from a 13-country list.

**Rice** — over 1,000 mm or irrigated: West Bengal, UP, Punjab (though Punjab is climatically unsuited, sustained by free power and MSP). **Wheat** — 50-75 cm and cool winters: UP, MP, Punjab. **Cotton** — black soil: Gujarat, Maharashtra, Telangana. **Sugarcane** — UP (largest area) but **Maharashtra has higher recovery**. **Tea** — well-drained slopes, Assam and Darjeeling; **coffee** — Karnataka (~70%), grown under shade. **Jute** — West Bengal, needing high humidity and retting water.

**North-Eastern Plateau (Chota Nagpur)** — the richest: iron ore, coal, manganese, bauxite, mica; **South-Western (Karnataka-Goa)** — iron and manganese but little coal; **North-Western (Rajasthan-Gujarat)** — non-ferrous (zinc, copper), petroleum. Coal: **Gondwana (~98% of reserves, Jharkhand-Odisha-Chhattisgarh-WB) versus Tertiary (Assam, Meghalaya)**. India imports nearly all its **cobalt, lithium, nickel and most copper** — hence the **30 critical minerals list**, the **National Critical Mineral Mission (₹16,300 crore)** and **KABIL** for overseas assets.

**Weber's least-cost theory** (transport, labour, agglomeration) and **Losch's market-area** approach. Indian instances: iron and steel at raw-material sites (Jamshedpur, Bhilai, Rourkela), **cotton textiles at the market and port (Mumbai, Ahmedabad)**, sugar shifting to Maharashtra for **higher sucrose recovery and cooperative organisation**, IT at **footloose** knowledge locations (Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune) where the input is human capital.

**Ring of Fire** (75% of the world's volcanoes); **Sahel** (desertification, Great Green Wall); **Amazon** (deforestation and the 'flying rivers'); **Arctic** (sea-ice loss, the Northern Sea Route, India's **Himadri station and Arctic Policy 2022**); **Antarctica** (Maitri, Bharati, and the new Maitri-II; the Antarctic Treaty and India's **Antarctic Act, 2022**); **Strait chokepoints** — Hormuz (~20% of world oil), Malacca (India's 'Malacca dilemma'), Bab-el-Mandeb (Red Sea shipping disruption), Suez and Panama (drought-driven transit cuts).

**Demographic transition** — India is in **Stage 3**, with TFR at 1.9 and falling; the **demographic dividend window runs to ~2055**, peaking in the 2030s, and is **state-asymmetric**: Kerala and Tamil Nadu have aged while Bihar and UP are still young — which makes **internal migration the mechanism that redistributes the dividend**, and delimitation the political flashpoint.

**Primate city** (Kolkata, Chennai in their regions), **rank-size rule**, **conurbation** (Delhi NCR), **million-plus cities: 53 in 2011, projected 68-70 by 2031**, **census towns**, **peri-urban interface**, **urban heat island** (Delhi's core runs several degrees above its periphery), and **urban flooding** — Chennai 2015, Mumbai 2005 and 2021, Bengaluru 2022 — caused by encroached wetlands and stormwater drains, addressed by the **NDMA Urban Flooding Guidelines (2010)**, the first of their kind in the world.

sections.h: Judgments, Statutes and Schemes for GS-1

groups.g: Judgments a society answer can carry

items.d: A **daughter is a coparcener by birth** under the amended Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act — the right is unobstructed heritage, so it applies whether or not the father was alive on 9 September 2005. The single best citation for women's land and property rights.

*Shayara Bano* struck down **instant triple talaq** as manifestly arbitrary (codified in the 2019 Act); *Shah Bano* granted maintenance under **Section 125 CrPC**, was reversed by the 1986 Act, and then substantially restored by *Danial Latifi* (2001). Together they are the standing example of the **personal law versus gender justice** conflict.

*Lata Singh* — an adult woman is free to marry whom she chooses, and **inter-caste marriage deserves state protection, not harassment**. *Shakti Vahini* — laid down preventive, remedial and punitive measures against **honour killings and khap panchayats**, holding that **'the consent of the family, community or clan is not necessary'** for a marriage between two consenting adults.

*Shirur Mutt* created the **essential religious practices** doctrine; *Sabarimala* held the exclusion of women aged 10-50 was not essential and violated Articles 14, 15, 17, 21 and 25, holding that **constitutional morality prevails over social morality** — with Justice Indu Malhotra's dissent on the limits of judicial review of faith. Pending before a nine-judge bench.

items.t: Suchita Srivastava (2009) and the MTP amendments
items.d: **Reproductive choice is part of personal liberty under Article 21** — a woman's right to make reproductive decisions cannot be overridden without her consent. The **MTP (Amendment) Act, 2021** extended the limit to **24 weeks** for specified categories, allowed unmarried women's access (by replacing 'husband' with 'partner'), and created **Medical Boards** for foetal-abnormality cases beyond 24 weeks.

*NALSA* recognised **transgender persons as a third gender** with a right to **self-identification**; *Navtej Johar* decriminalised consensual same-sex relations. *Supriyo* (2023) declined to recognise same-sex marriage, leaving it to Parliament while directing a **committee on the rights of queer couples** — the current position.

*Indra Sawhney* — caste can be a starting point for identifying a backward class, the **creamy layer** must be excluded, and reservation is capped at **50%** save in extraordinary circumstances. *Davinder Singh* (2024) permitted **sub-classification within Scheduled Castes**, overruling *E.V. Chinnaiah* — the key development for the 'heterogeneity within backwardness' argument.

items.t: Aligarh Muslim University (2024) and T.M.A. Pai (2002)
